about.title: Quadratic Models: Balls, Pens and Profit
about.length_note: About 40 minutes. There are three settings (a thrown ball, an area problem, a profit problem), and each needs about 10 minutes to explain, try and check. It splits easily: do the ball in one sitting, then the pen and the profit in another.

sources.title: 9.5 Solve Applications of Quadratic Equations, Intermediate Algebra 2e
7.6.3 Using Quadratic Functions to Describe Height, Algebra 1
Quadratic Functions (chapter 29), Algebra and Trigonometry OpenStax, Pressbooks edition
Height of a Projectile (college algebra modeling exercise)

say.text: Hi, {name}. Today we use quadratics to describe real things: a thrown ball, a fenced pen and a game night's profit.

show.text: Quadratic Models

say.text: We'll do three jobs again and again. Find the highest or lowest point. Find where the answer is zero. Check that the answers make sense.

show.text: 1. Find the top or bottom (the vertex). 2. Find the zeros. 3. Check the answers fit the story.

say.text: A model is an equation that matches a real situation. Ours will all be quadratics.

show.text: Model: an equation that describes a real situation

say.text: First, a reminder. The vertex is the turning point of a parabola. If the parabola opens down, the vertex is the highest point, the maximum. If it opens up, the vertex is the lowest point, the minimum.

show.text: Vertex: the turning point. Opens down = maximum. Opens up = minimum.

ask.q: A parabola opens downward. What is its vertex?
wrong: The spot where it crosses the x-axis
ask.why: Opening down is like a hill. The top of the hill is the vertex, so it is the maximum.

say.text: To find where the vertex is, use x = −b ÷ 2a. That gives the left-to-right spot. Then put that number back into the equation to get the height.

show.text: Vertex spot: x = −b ÷ 2a. Then find y by plugging x back in.

say.text: Now a ball. For something thrown straight up, its height in feet is −16t² plus the starting speed times t, plus the starting height.

show.text: h = −16t² + v₀t + h₀ | t = seconds, v₀ = starting upward speed (ft/s), h₀ = starting height (ft)

say.text: The plain number at the end is the starting height. At t = 0 every t-term disappears. If you work in meters, the −16 becomes −4.9.

show.text: Feet: −16t². Meters: −4.9t².

ask.q: A ball has height H(t) = −16t² + 80t + 40. How high is it at t = 0?
ask.why: At t = 0 the −16t² and 80t parts are both zero. Only the 40 is left, and that is the starting height.

say.text: Here is Sam's ball: H(t) = −16t² + 80t + 40, thrown up from a balcony 40 feet high. See the arch? It is a mirror image. At 2 seconds and 3 seconds the height is the same, 136 feet.

show.text: Height of the ball over time

say.text: When is the ball highest? At the vertex. t = −80 ÷ (2 × −16) = 2.5 seconds.

show.text: 2.5 seconds

ask.q: Another ball has height h(t) = −16t² + 64t + 80. At what time is it highest?
ask.why: t = −64 ÷ (2 × −16) = −64 ÷ −32 = 2. The two negatives cancel, so the answer is positive.

say.text: How high is it then? Put 2.5 back in: −16(6.25) + 200 + 40 = 140. The ball peaks at 140 feet.

show.text: 140 feet

ask.q: The vertex is (2.5, 140). What does the 140 tell us?
ask.right: The highest height the ball reaches, in feet
wrong: How many seconds the ball stays in the air
The height the ball starts at
ask.why: The first number of the vertex is the time. The second number is the height at that time, so 140 is the maximum height.

say.text: When does the ball land? When its height is zero. So we solve −16t² + 80t + 40 = 0.

show.text: On the ground means height = 0

say.text: The quadratic formula gives two answers: t ≈ 5.46 and t ≈ −0.46. A quadratic often gives two answers, but only one may fit the story.

ask.q: Which answer is the time the ball lands?
ask.why: The clock starts at the throw, t = 0, so a negative time is before the throw. 2.5 seconds is the peak, not the landing.

say.text: Intercepts have meanings too. The height when t = 0 is the starting height. The positive t-intercept is the landing time.

show.text: y-intercept (t = 0): starting height, 40 ft | positive t-intercept: landing time, about 5.46 s

say.text: So always check: does this answer fit the story? Time can't be negative. A length can't be zero or negative. A price can't be negative.

show.text: Time ≥ 0. Length > 0. Price ≥ 0. Reject answers that break the story.

say.text: Try one. A rocket model starts 384 feet up: h(t) = −16t² + 80t + 384. Setting h = 0 gives t = −3 or t = 8.

ask.why: −3 is before the launch, so we reject it. 8 seconds is the only time that fits.

say.text: Now no ball at all. You have 40 feet of fence for a rectangular pen. Which size gives the most room? The fence goes all the way around, so length plus width is 20.

show.text: A rectangular pen on grass with fence on all four sides. The short side is labeled w. The long side is labeled 20 − w.

ask.q: The width is 6 feet. What is the length?
ask.why: Length + width = 20, so the length is 20 − 6 = 14.

say.text: Area is width times length: A = w(20 − w) = −w² + 20w. The leading number is negative, so the parabola opens down. The vertex is the maximum area.

show.text: A = −w² + 20w. Opens down, so the vertex is the maximum.

say.text: The vertex is at w = −20 ÷ (2 × −1) = 10. Then A = 10 × 10 = 100 square feet. The best pen is a square.

show.text: 10 ft by 10 ft = 100 sq ft

ask.q: Which pen has the most area with 40 feet of fence?
ask.why: All of them use 40 feet of fence, but the vertex gives the biggest area. Each of the others is smaller than 100.

say.text: The zeros of A = −w² + 20w are w = 0 and w = 20. At those widths the area is zero. So a sensible width is between 0 and 20.

show.text: Reasonable widths: 0 < w < 20

ask.q: Is a width of 25 feet reasonable for this pen?
ask.right: No, because the length would be −5 feet
wrong: Yes, because 25 is a positive number
Yes, because it is bigger than 20
No, because 25 is not a whole number
ask.why: The length is 20 − 25 = −5, and a length can't be negative. The width has to stay between 0 and 20.

say.text: Last setting: profit. Set a ticket price too low and you earn little. Set it too high and nobody comes. So profit rises, then falls, like a hill.

show.text: Profit = money in − money out

say.text: Here are made-up numbers. Sam's club sells tickets to a game night. P(x) = −5x² + 100x − 180, where x is the ticket price in dollars. The vertex is at x = 10, and P(10) = 320.

show.text: Profit at different ticket prices (made-up example)

ask.q: What ticket price gives the most profit?
ask.why: The x-value of the vertex is the price, $10. The $320 is the profit at that price.

say.text: Now the zeros. Factor: −5(x − 2)(x − 18) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 18. These are the break-even prices. At those prices you earn exactly nothing.

show.text: Break-even at $2 | Break-even at $18

ask.q: Which ticket prices make a profit?
ask.why: The parabola is above zero between the two zeros. Outside them the club loses money.

say.text: Some models have a minimum. Say a server's cost per hour is C(x) = 2x² − 24x + 100, where x is hundreds of players. The vertex is at x = 6 and C(6) = 28, so the lowest cost is $28.

show.text: Opens up: the vertex is the minimum. C(6) = 28

ask.q: Why is the vertex of C(x) = 2x² − 24x + 100 a minimum?
ask.right: The leading number 2 is positive, so the parabola opens up
ask.why: A positive leading number opens the parabola up. The vertex is then the lowest point.

say.text: Here is the whole routine. Read what the letters mean. Find the vertex with −b ÷ 2a. Plug in for the max or min. Set the output to zero for intercepts. Then throw out answers that don't fit the story.

show.text: 1. Read the story. 2. x = −b ÷ 2a. 3. Plug in for the max or min. 4. Set to 0 for zeros. 5. Check each answer fits.

say.text: One last check, all on your own. A ball has h(t) = −16t² + 32t + 48. Setting h = 0 gives t² − 2t − 3 = 0, which factors as (t − 3)(t + 1) = 0.

show.text: h(t) = −16t² + 32t + 48. Find the landing time.

ask.why: The zeros are t = 3 and t = −1. A time of −1 is before the throw, so we reject it. 1 second is the vertex time, not the landing.

say.text: Well done, {name}. Quadratic models are just three questions: how high or low, where is it zero, and does that answer make sense? Next class we compare linear, exponential and quadratic functions side by side.

show.text: Top or bottom. Zeros. Does it fit?

other_side.claim: The formula h = −16t² + v₀t + h₀ tells exactly how high a thrown ball goes.
other_side.other_view: It is a simplified model. Textbook versions of it ignore air resistance, so a real ball, especially a light or fast one, will not follow the curve exactly.
